summary: James Murdoch worked in Japanology and history and archaeology. He studied at the University of Aberdeen (ca. 1875–1879) and under Theodor Benfey (ca. 1877–1878), and later held posts at the University of Tokyo, Kanazawa University, and Kagoshima University.

James Prinsep was an Indologist and historian. He served as Assistant Assay-Master and Assay-Master at the India Government Mint in Kolkata and Benares, directed The Asiatic Society (1832–1838), and founded the Journal of the Asiatic Society of Bengal.

James Rennell worked in history, archaeology, and Indology. He served in the Bengal Engineers and as a surveyor in Bengal for the East India Company (1764–1777), later founding the Royal Geographical Society in 1830.

James Robert Ballantyne worked in Indology, philosophy, and linguistics. He studied at Edinburgh, East India Company College, and Glasgow (Ph.D.), later serving as Principal of Benares Sanskrit College, Professor at King's College London, and librarian at the India Office.

James Robson specializes in Buddhist studies, Sinology, and religious studies. Educated at UC Santa Barbara and Stanford (Ph.D. ca. 2002), he taught at Williams College and the University of Michigan before becoming a professor at Harvard and director of the Harvard-Yenching Institute.

James Roland Ware specialized in Sinology, Buddhist studies, and Indology, studying at the University of Pennsylvania and under Franklin Edgerton and Sylvain Lévi. He held teaching posts at Lehigh, the University of Washington, and Harvard University.

James Smith Reid was a scholar of history and archaeology who studied at the University of Cambridge. He held academic posts across Cambridge at Christ's College (1869–1880), Pembroke College (1873–1885), and Gonville and Caius College (1878–1926).

James Stark was a scholar of history, archaeology, and Indology. He served as a Puisne Justice on the Supreme Court of Sri Lanka in 1840 and as President of the Royal Asiatic Society of Sri Lanka in 1845.

James Stewart King was a scholar in the fields of Iranian and Central Asian studies as well as history and archaeology. He completed his education at Trinity College Dublin and the Royal Military Academy Sandhurst.

James Sutherland Cotton was an Indologist and historian who completed his education at Trinity College, Oxford. He served as a Fellow and Lecturer at Queen's College, Benares, and held a post at Queens' College from 1871 to 1874.

James Taft Hatfield was a linguist and Indologist who earned his degrees from Northwestern and Johns Hopkins, with studies in Germany and Oxford. He taught at Rust College and served as a professor at Northwestern University from 1890 to 1934.

James Talboys Wheeler was an Indologist and historian. He served as Professor of Moral and Mental Philosophy at Presidency College, Chennai (ca. 1858–1862) and as Assistant Secretary to the Government of India (ca. 1867–1875).
James Thomas Molesworth was an Indologist and linguist. He served professionally as a linguist with the Bombay Native Infantry in 1814 and with the Commissariat Department.

James Tod worked in history, archaeology, and Indology, studying at the Royal Military Academy, Woolwich, and under Gyanchandra. He served with the East India Company (ca. 1799–1823) and as Librarian of the Royal Asiatic Society (ca. 1823–1835).
James W. Benson is an Indologist and linguist. He has held academic posts at Harvard University (attested 1999), the University of Oxford (attested 1999), and Wolfson College, Oxford (attested 2001).

James W. Heisig is a scholar in philosophy, religious studies, and Japanology who earned a PhD from Cambridge in 1973. He served at Divine Word College and spent much of his career at Nanzan University and its Institute for Religion and Culture.

James Ward was a philosopher who was educated at Mostyn House School, Fitzwilliam College, and Trinity College, Cambridge. He subsequently held an academic post at the University of Cambridge from ca. 1897 to 1925.
James Whitehill is a scholar of Buddhist studies, religious studies, and philosophy. He served as Professor of Religion at Stephens College (attested 2000) and founded the Columbia Zen Center.

James Wilkinson Breeks was an Indology and history and archaeology scholar who studied at the East India Company College from ca. 1850 to 1852. He subsequently served in the Indian Civil Service from ca. 1852 to 1872.
James Wilson was an Indologist and linguist. He studied at the University of Edinburgh and Balliol College, Oxford, and served as a civil servant in the Indian Civil Service from 1873 to 1910.
